stories.headline: Cyclone Murasu approaches Andhra coast; Odisha, Tamil Nadu issue alerts
stories.title: Cyclone Murasu approaches Andhra coast; Odisha, Tamil Nadu issue alerts
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has forecast wind speeds of 100–110 kmph, gusting up to 120 kmph, during landfall.
The system is expected to intensify into a severe cyclonic storm before crossing the coast.

Amaravati/Bhubaneswar/Chennai: Andhra Pradesh, Odisha and Tamil Nadu have stepped up precautionary measures as Cyclone Murasu intensified over the Bay of Bengal and is expected to cross the south Andhra Pradesh coast between Nellore and Narsapur during the night of November 2 and the early hours of November 3.
The approaching storm has prompted Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N Chandrababu Naidu to direct officials to remain prepared for rescue and relief operations.
Odisha has sounded a high alert in its southern districts, while Tamil Nadu has asked district collectors to remain vigilant in view of the forecast of heavy to very heavy rainfall.
Naidu on Sunday directed officials to ensure that adequate personnel and equipment were available for rescue and relief operations in vulnerable areas.
He also asked them to prepare timelines for restoring electricity in the event of damage to power infrastructure and communicate the information to the public.

"Another cyclone is approaching Andhra Pradesh and officials must remain fully prepared to undertake relief and rescue operations, as a severe cyclonic storm is expected to cross the coast near Bapatla on the morning of November 3," said Naidu in an official press release.
Officials told the Chief Minister that the system was expected to intensify into a cyclonic storm and subsequently strengthen into a severe cyclonic storm over the west-central Bay of Bengal.
Several coastal districts are likely to receive moderate to heavy rainfall on November 2, with isolated extremely heavy showers.
Heavy to very heavy rainfall is forecast in parts of the state on November 3 and 4.
Eluru, Krishna, NTR, West Godavari, Guntur and Bapatla are among the districts expected to receive significant rainfall.

stories.title: Cyclone Murasu: Orange alert in six Telangana districts, yellow alert in five on November 2

article_sentences: With Cyclone Murasu, which is likely to cross Andhra Pradesh coast on the morning of Tuesday (November 3), the India Meteorological Department (IMD) has issued an orange alert in six Telangana districts and a yellow alert in five districts for Monday (November 2).
According to the IMD’s latest bulletin, an orange alert, meaning heavy to very heavy rainfall, has been issued in Khammam, Nalgonda, Suryapet, Mahabubnagar, Nagarkurnool and Wanaparthy districts.
Additionally, a yellow alert, meaning heavy rainfall, has been issued in Jangaon, Yadadri Bhuvanagiri, Rangareddy, Hyderabad and Medchal Malkajgiri districts.
Hyderabad and its surrounding areas for the next 24 hours will see a partly cloudy sky.
“Light to moderate rain or thundershowers with lightning accompanied by gusty winds are very likely to occur in parts of the city.
The maximum and minimum temperatures are likely to be around 34C and 24C respectively,” the bulletin said.

stories.headline: Deep depression in Bay of Bengal intensifies into cyclone ‘Murasu’
stories.title: Deep depression in Bay of Bengal intensifies into cyclone ‘Murasu’
stories.summary: The cyclone, which has been given the name ‘Murasu’, is likely to intensify into a severe cyclone and cross the Andhra Pradesh coast on November 2-3.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The cyclone, which has been given the name ‘Murasu’, is likely to intensify into a severe cyclone and cross the Andhra Pradesh coast on November 2-3.

Amaravati: The India Meteorological Department (IMD) on Sunday issued a cyclone alert for Andhra Pradesh and adjoining north Tamil Nadu coasts as the deep depression in the Bay of Bengal has intensified into a cyclonic storm.
The IMD said in a bulletin on Sunday afternoon that a deep depression intensified into cyclonic storm ‘Murasu’ over southwest & adjoining west-central Bay of Bengal.

The deep depression moved west-northwestwards with speed of 23 kmph during past 6 hours, intensified into the cyclonic storm ‘Murasu’ and lay centered at 11.30 a.m. IST of Sunday over southwest & adjoining westcentral Bay of Bengal, about 560 km east-southeast of Chennai (Tamil Nadu), 660 km south-southeast of Vishakhapatnam (Andhra Pradesh), 630 km east-southeast of Nellore (Andhra Pradesh), 640 km southeast of Machilipatnam (Andhra Pradesh) and 680 km east-southeast of Ongole (Andhra Pradesh).
It is very likely to move west-northwestwards and intensify further into a severe cyclonic storm over the west-central Bay of Bengal around Monday morning.

Thereafter, it is very likely to move northwestwards and cross the south Andhra Pradesh coast as a severe cyclonic storm with wind speed of 100 to 110 kmph gusting 120kmph between Nellore and Narsapur during midnight (2330 Hrs IST) of 2nd to early hours (0400 Hrs IST) on Tuesday.
This will be the second cyclonic storm to cross the Andhra Pradesh coast in less than a week.
Very severe cyclonic storm ‘Arnab’ crossed the Andhra Pradesh coast near Narsapur in the early hours of October 28, with the maximum sustained wind speed of 125-135 kmph gusting to 150 kmph.
It claimed seven lives and caused widespread damage to crops, roads, electricity and telecom infrastructure in the coastal districts.
Crops over thousands of acres were damaged in the cyclone while hundreds of electricity polls and trees were uprooted.
As per preliminary estimates, the cyclone caused losses of Rs 4,600 crore.
A Central team is currently visiting the state to assess the damage caused by the cyclone.

stories.headline: Army's peacetime role as important as its wartime contribution: Jitendra Singh
stories.title: Army's peacetime role as important as its wartime contribution: Jitendra Singh
stories.summary: Jammu, Nov 1: Underscoring the Army's invaluable contribution beyond its conventional role of safeguarding the nation's borders, Union minister Jitendra Singh on Sunday said its role during peacetime was as important as its contribution during war. He particularly highlighted the Army's efforts to assist civilians in remote and geographically challenging areas through humanitarian initiatives, disaster relief and healthcare outreach. Singh, the Minister of State in the Prime Minister's Office, was speaking to reporters after inaugurating a two-day mega medical camp organized by the Army under Operation Sadbhavana at its Advanced Landing Ground (ALG) in Kishtwar district of Jammu and Kashmir. The medical camp is expected to benefit around 5,000 people by providing access to specialist doctors, free diagnostic facilities, medicines and assistive aids. The camp also features ABHA registration facilities, dedicated welfare stalls for Veer Naris and ex-servicemen, a youth guidance stall, besides awareness stalls set up by banks and various government departments. Singh appreciated the coordinated efforts of the Army, specialist doctors, civilian medical practitioners, chief medical officers and the local administration in organising the camp and said such initiatives are particularly important for rural and remote areas where access to specialised healthcare facilities remains limited. He pointed out that several diseases, which can be prevented or treated through timely intervention, often go undiagnosed because people living in far-flung villages are unaware of their medical conditions. “One of the distinguishing features of this camp is that it offers several medical specialities that are otherwise not readily available in this area. There are many diseases that can be prevented, but people living in remote villages often remain unaware of their conditions. As a result, these ailments sometimes reach a serious stage before they seek medical attention,” the minister said. Highlighting the importance of eye care, he said a considerable number of patients attending the camp were found to be suffering from cataracts, many of whom had not been aware of their condition. “In medical terminology, cataract is considered a preventable cause of blindness. In today's world, nobody should lose their eyesight because of cataracts. If that happens, it is certainly not a good reflection of our healthcare system,” he remarked. Singh said such medical camps serve a dual purpose: providing immediate medical assistance to people while also generating valuable information about the prevalence of diseases and the specific healthcare requirements of different areas. He said the initiative had been started earlier this year with a particular focus on rural and geographically challenging regions where all medical specialities and healthcare facilities are not readily available. “Based on the findings of these camps, we prepare a report and share it with the civilian authorities and the chief medical officer. This helps them understand which diseases are more prevalent in particular areas and what kind of specialised medical facilities are required there,” he said. The Union minister also underlined the Indian Army's contribution beyond its conventional role of safeguarding the country's borders and maintaining security, particularly in regions that have witnessed difficult geographical conditions and security challenges. “The Army is active during wartime, and its activities naturally receive considerable media attention. However, its contribution during peacetime, particularly in our region, is equally invaluable. “Whether it is a flood, an outbreak of disease, or a medical camp like this, the Army always comes forward to help. In these mountainous and remote areas, which have also witnessed the shadow of terrorism, the Army not only protects the people but also extends valuable assistance to the local population,” the Udhampur MP said. The minister expressed satisfaction over the response received during the initial hours and said "I am confident that more than 5,000 people will benefit from the services being provided over two days." The two-day medical camp under Operation Sadbhavana reflects the Army's continued efforts to supplement civilian healthcare services and extend specialised medical assistance to people living in geographically challenging areas of Jammu and Kashmir, an Army spokesman said. With specialist consultations, diagnostic facilities, free medicines, dental procedures and various welfare and awareness initiatives under one roof, the camp is aimed at improving access to healthcare while strengthening coordination between the Army, civil administration and the health department, he said.

stories.title: CJI to HCs: Why make litigants rush to Supreme Court for early hearings
stories.summary: Chief Justice of India Surya Kant asks ‘Can we ensure that a litigant’s access to timely justice does not depend upon their ability to travel to the national capital?’

article_sentences: Chief Justice of India Surya Kant on Sunday (November 1, 2026) flagged a “growing tendency” among litigants to approach the Supreme Court with requests to speed up justice delivery in State High Courts.

“We are witnessing a growing tendency of litigants approaching the Supreme Court requesting directions for urgent listing or early hearing of matters pending before the High Courts,” Chief Justice Kant said in an address at the Kerala High Court.
His remarks are significant, as 65,54,788 cases are pending in High Courts across the country.
The pendency in the Supreme Court is dangerously close to an unprecedented one-lakh mark, with a backlog hovering at 97,201 cases.
The increase in the number of judges from 34 to 38 (including the Chief Justice of India) has not stemmed the steady northward progress of pendency.
The 25 High Courts have 292 judicial vacancies against a total sanctioned strength of 1,122 as on October 6, 2026.

“The Supreme Court has consistently respected the institutional autonomy of High Courts, including their authority to regulate their own rosters...

stories.headline: CJI Surya Kant calls for introspection on need to improve responsiveness of judicial process
stories.title: CJI Surya Kant calls for introspection on need to improve responsiveness of judicial process
stories.summary: Kochi, Nov 1: Chief Justice of India Surya Kant on Sunday called for introspection on whether there is room to improve the responsiveness of the judicial process in view of the growing tendency among litigants to move the Supreme Court for urgent listing or early hearing of matters pending before the High Courts. CJI Kant said that the apex court has as consistently respected the institutional autonomy of High Courts, including their authority to regulate their own rosters, but the frequency of such requests invites us to consider whether there is room to improve the responsiveness of our processes. "We must ask ourselves -- can urgent matters be identified more effectively? Can listing procedures be made more transparent and predictable? Can technology assist in prioritising cases where delay may cause irreversible prejudice? "And can we ensure that a litigant’s access to timely justice does not depend upon their ability to travel to the national capital?" were queries he posed during his inaugural address on the occasion of the platinum jubilee anniversary celebrations of the Kerala High Court here. Justice Kant said that constitutional justice in India does not begin and end in New Delhi as its strength lies in a robust network of 25 constitutional High Courts spread across the country, "each entrusted with the duty of protecting rights and upholding the rule of law". He said that the High Courts remain closely connected to the everyday realities of the people as they understand the language of local grievances, the circumstances of regional communities, and the practical consequences of governmental action. He further said that under Article 226 of the Constitution, the High Courts have a wide canvas "to fashion meaningful remedies across diverse legal, statutory, administrative and contractual disputes". "Equally important is their power to grant timely interim protection. Sometimes, the difference between justice and injustice lies not in the final judgment, but in whether the court intervenes when intervention is most needed," the CJI said in his address. Referring to the Kerala High Court's seven decade long history, Justice Kant said that the High Court and the state of Keralam were both formed in 1956 and their journey during the last 70 years was closely intertwined with each other. He said that the court played a vital role in the state's constitutional development. "Through its decisions, it has helped translate constitutional principles into lived realities, ensuring that the rights and liberties of citizens remain protected and that public power is exercised within the bounds of law," the CJI said. He said that the Kerala HC's history did not begin with the formation of the state, rather it inherited a centuries old "rich judicial tradition" from the regions that now constitute Keralam. "From the early courts of Travancore and Cochin, to the establishment of the Travancore High Court in 1887 and the Travancore-Cochin High Court in 1949, each successive institution contributed to the foundations upon which the present Court was built," Justice Kant said. He said that the progressive spirit of the High Court was evident in its constitutional jurisprudence. "Whether through its extensive engagement with doctrines of environmental protection, or its invocation of fundamental rights to safeguard life and personal liberty, this High Court has repeatedly demonstrated that constitutional promises must find expression in everyday realities," he said. The CJI said that one example of this was the High Court's 1999 order prohibiting smoking in public places, the first constitutional court to do so across the world. "It was a remarkable instance of constitutional foresight, where the Court did not wait for society to catch up with the law, but used the law to show society the way forward," he said. He said that Keralam has long demonstrated that progress is sustained through the combined strength of education, social awareness and public participation. Justice Kant said that just like Keralam's backwaters, where countless streams and waterways ultimately sustain one interconnected ecosystem, the constitutional courts in India too must retain their individual authority while working in harmony towards a shared purpose.

Kochi, Nov 1: Chief Justice of India Surya Kant on Sunday called for introspection on whether there is room to improve the responsiveness of the judicial process in view of the growing tendency among litigants to move the Supreme Court for urgent listing or early hearing of matters pending before the High Courts.

Referring to the Kerala High Court's seven decade long history, Justice Kant said that the High Court and the state of Keralam were both formed in 1956 and their journey during the last 70 years was closely intertwined with each other.

"From the early courts of Travancore and Cochin, to the establishment of the Travancore High Court in 1887 and the Travancore-Cochin High Court in 1949, each successive institution contributed to the foundations upon which the present Court was built," Justice Kant said.

stories.headline: Jio says tariff hikes can wait, eyes 10-15 partners for overseas play
stories.title: Jio says tariff hikes can wait, eyes 10-15 partners for overseas play
stories.summary: Jio Platforms plans to drive growth through digital services and overseas technology partnerships rather than rely solely on mobile tariff hikes.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Fresh from its stock market debut, Jio Platforms is looking beyond mobile tariff hikes to drive revenue growth, with plans to expand its digital services business and take its technology overseas.

Jio does not want to rely solely on charging subscribers more and will decide on tariff increases at an apt time, depending on market conditions and the broader economic environment, the company's management told analysts on Friday.
“As a company, we don't want to use that (tariff hike) as the only lever of growth.
What we want, we have capability of creating a technological layer, we want to stress that as a more sustainable way of doing it,” managing director Akash Ambani said.
The statement assumes significance as it has been over 2.5 years since telecom operators took an across-the-board increase in headline tariffs.
Analysts and investors have been speculating a tariff hike for over a year now, as it is seen necessary to boost return on capital employed for the operators.
And now, after the listing of Jio Platforms, analysts are indicating a nearly 15% hike in the current fiscal year.
Tariff hikes are key to boost the average revenue per user (Arpu) of operators, a critical metric that measures the average revenue generated per subscriber.
Higher tariffs help operators improve revenue growth, profitability and cash flows.

“We want to focus on how we are adding more value to customers and thereby increasing the realization that we have from the customers,” Anshuman Thakur, chief strategy officer of Jio Platforms said during the call, adding that the company wants to focus much more on the digital services that it is offering to the customers.
“Even today, if you look at our growth trajectory, Arpu has grown by almost 3.5%.
Around 4-5% growth in Arpu just because of customer mix changing, people consuming more is happening organically," Thakur said.
